findings.description: The inline policy grants wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's long-lived key would permit full control of compute, storage, and serverless resources account-wide, enabling S3 data exfiltration and privilege escalation by creating or updating Lambda functions and EC2 instances that carry existing IAM roles.

A permanent IAM access key is provisioned for a highly privileged service user with no rotation mechanism, instead of an IAM role issuing temporary STS credentials. Long-lived keys are a durable, frequently leaked credential vector.

No pgp_key is supplied, so the secret access key is written to the Terraform state file in plaintext (the encrypted_secret attribute will be empty). Anyone with read access to the state backend obtains a credential with near-full ec2/s3/lambda privileges.
Access key material is exported as a root module output without sensitive = true, so it can be rendered in plan/apply output, CI logs, and read by any module consumer via `terraform output`.

findings.issue_category: privileged user without boundary or MFA
findings.description: A service principal is modelled as an IAM user with static keys rather than an assumable role, and has neither a permissions boundary nor any MFA condition constraining use of its credentials, leaving no upper bound or second factor on the wildcard privileges it holds.

The IAM username of the highly privileged deploy user is exported as a non-sensitive output, disclosing a valid principal name that aids targeted credential attacks against the account. Low impact relative to the key material exposure.
